Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the labs at Dreamworks Animation, and it's out to devour your kids. Susan, aka "Ginormica," has to save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens." But don't be too alarmed. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless -- a toothless satire with a knee-jerk feminist theme and a sorry excuse for a plot. That sounds harsh, I know. Who doesn't want to see a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles -- the ultimate demolition roller derby? But think about that, just for a second. Roller skates work because they have fixed wheels. Try it with motorcars and you won't get very far. Is that too picky? Perhaps, but you wouldn't find Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that kind of inattention to detail is typical of the lackadaisical storytelling here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (The talent pool for this one includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale" and the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker," incidentally.) High concepts, top-notch voice talent and scattershot pop cultural references are no compensation for a coherent script. The XXXL lady in question -- dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards -- starts out plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite hits her just minutes before she's supposed to tie the knot with unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her rapid growth spurt saves her from that particular fate worse than death, even if at first glance her new roommates don't look like much of an improvement. There's Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated with a bug; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen) an amorphous blue jelly-like blob who gets on just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who's all mouth; and a giant dust mite called Insectosaurus who isn't voiced by anyone because he doesn't have anything to say. Sci-fi fans will have fun counting off the references to myriad classics -- "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra" and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," for starters -- and noting a few clever bits and pieces (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove"). The trouble is, once the introductions are over, the filmmakers can only launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squidlike creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, and a one-eyed tin robot to do his dirty work for him. Ginormica gets a kick-butt finale, and is a much stronger character -- in any number of ways -- than the movie's president. (In a genuinely witty casting touch he's voiced by Stephen Colbert.) That may be good politics or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective -- it's been awhile since a family animated feature produced a genuinely strong female character (unless you count "Coraline," which was way too scary for my family) -- but Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time coming. iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'? (Bizarrely -- and maybe it's just my imagination -- Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. I wonder ... would that make Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?) Visually, too, "Monsters vs Aliens" is undistinguished, although its shortcomings may be disguised if you seek out the 3-D version. Funny how 3-D movies tend to produce two-dimensional characters, with "Coraline" again the exception to the rule. Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" should be a lot of fun -- and it is, in places. But the truth is it's as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiance. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps." "Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- Watch out! Lock up your loved ones! Yet another bloated, over-produced, high-concept monstrosity has escaped from the laboratories at Dreamworks Animation, and it has set its sights on devouring your children. Susan, better known as "Ginormica," must save the world in "Monsters vs. Aliens."

But there is no cause for undue alarm. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is relatively harmless—a toothless satire burdened by a knee-jerk feminist theme and a woefully inadequate plot. I know that sounds harsh. After all, who wouldn't relish the sight of a 50-foot woman careening through San Francisco on skates that turn out to be automobiles—the ultimate demolition roller derby? Yet consider that image, if only for a moment. Roller skates function precisely because they have fixed wheels. Attempt the same feat with motorcars, and you won't get very far.

Is that too pedantic? Perhaps. But you would never catch Pixar playing so fast and loose with the laws of physics, and that sort of inattention to detail is emblematic of the lackadaisical storytelling both here and in other Dreamworks animated features. (Incidentally, the talent behind this project includes the directors of "Shrek 2" and "Shark Tale," along with the writers of "Kung Fu Panda" and "The Rocker.") High concepts, top-notch voice talent, and scattershot pop-cultural references are no substitute for a coherent script.

The XXXL lady in question—dubbed "Ginormica" by her U.S. military guards—begins as the plain and petite Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), until a meteorite strikes her mere minutes before she is set to tie the knot with the unctuous chauvinist Derek (Paul Rudd). Her sudden growth spurt spares her from that particular fate worse than death, though at first glance her new roommates hardly seem an improvement. There is Dr. Cockroach (Hugh Laurie), a mad scientist who semi-advertently mutated himself with an insect; B.O.B. (Seth Rogen), an amorphous, blue, jelly-like blob who gets along just fine without a brain; Missing Link (Will Arnett), a gung-ho amphibian who is all mouth; and a giant dust mite named Insectosaurus, who is voiced by no one, for he has nothing to say.

Science-fiction fans will delight in tallying the references to countless classics—"Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Invaders from Mars," "The Fly," "The Creature from the Black Lagoon," "The Blob," "Mothra," and "Attack of the 50-Foot Woman," to name but a few—and in noting a few clever flourishes along the way (Kiefer Sutherland, as General W.R. Monger, riffs on George C. Scott in "Dr. Strangelove").

The trouble is that, once the introductions conclude, the filmmakers can do little more than launch their desperately limp plot: The White House turns to these monstrous superheroes to save the planet from the evil Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson), a squid-like creature with four eyes and twice as many legs, aided by a one-eyed tin robot who performs his dirty work.

Ginormica is granted a kick-butt finale, and she proves a far stronger character—in any number of ways—than the film's president. (In a genuinely witty stroke of casting, he is voiced by Stephen Colbert.) This may amount to shrewd politics, or at least a sound marketing decision from the studio's perspective—it has been quite some time since a family animated feature yielded a genuinely strong female character (unless one counts "Coraline," which proved far too frightening for my family). Even so, Susan's self-esteem is an awfully long time in coming.

iReport.com: What do you think of 'Monsters vs. Aliens'?

(Curiously—and perhaps it is merely my imagination—Gallaxhar bears a passing resemblance to President Obama. Which makes me wonder: would that render Susan/Ginormica a surrogate for Sarah Palin or Hillary Clinton?)

Visually, "Monsters vs. Aliens" is likewise undistinguished, though its shortcomings may be masked if you seek out the 3-D version. It is curious how 3-D films tend to produce two-dimensional characters—with "Coraline," once again, the exception that proves the rule.

Jocular and unpretentiously trashy, "Monsters vs. Aliens" ought to be a great deal of fun—and, in places, it is. But the truth is that the film is as hung up on itself as Susan's preening fiancé. Hand on heart, I had a better time at "Space Chimps."

"Monsters vs. Aliens" runs 94 minutes and is rated PG. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

# A Critical Look at "Monsters vs. Aliens"

Despite its considerable production values and ambitious high-concept premise, "Monsters vs. Aliens" ultimately fails to deliver where it matters most. The film is a slickly produced spectacle that dazzles the eye but leaves audiences wanting when it comes to storytelling, lacking both a coherent plot and any meaningful substance beneath its polished surface.

At its core, the film aspires to be a satire, but it registers as a decidedly toothless one. What might have been an opportunity for genuine wit and depth is squandered on a shallow, knee-jerk feminist theme that feels more like a superficial gesture than a thoughtfully developed message. Rather than exploring its ideas with nuance, the film settles for surface-level gestures that never earn the weight they seem to reach for.

Much of the blame falls on Dreamworks Animation, whose careless approach to storytelling stands in stark contrast to the meticulous craftsmanship of rival studio Pixar. Where Pixar consistently demonstrates a devotion to narrative integrity and attention to detail—including respect for basic principles like the laws of physics—Dreamworks appears content to disregard such considerations in favor of empty spectacle.

The plot centers on Susan Murphy, an ordinary young woman whose life takes an extraordinary turn when she is struck by a meteorite just moments before her wedding. The collision transforms her into a fifty-foot giant, earning her the nickname "Ginormica." Thrust into a strange new existence, Susan finds herself among an eccentric cast of monster companions, including the brilliant Dr. Cockroach, the gelatinous B.O.B., the amphibious Missing Link, and the towering Insectosaurus—a colorful ensemble brought to life by an impressive roster of voice talent.

Yet even with such a promising setup and capable performances, the film cannot overcome its fundamental shortcomings, remaining a visually accomplished but hollow experience.

# Monsters vs. Aliens: A Missed Opportunity

DreamWorks Animation's "Monsters vs. Aliens" arrives with all the trappings of a summer blockbuster—a stellar voice cast, cutting-edge 3D animation, and a premise ripe with comedic potential. The film centers on Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), an ordinary woman whose wedding day takes an extraordinary turn when she's struck by a mysterious meteorite. In an instant, she balloons to a staggering forty-nine feet, earning her the government-appointed moniker "Ginormica" and a one-way ticket to a top-secret facility where she's imprisoned alongside other captured creatures.

There, Susan meets her fellow misfits: the brilliant but insect-headed Dr. Cockroach, the gelatinous and dim-witted B.O.B., the fish-ape hybrid known as The Missing Link, and the enormous grub-like Insectosaurus. When an alien overlord named Gallaxhar launches an assault on Earth, this ragtag band of monsters is deployed as humanity's unlikely last line of defense, and Susan must embrace her newfound size and strength to save the world.

## The Problem with the Package

Yet for all its ambition and firepower, the film ultimately disappoints. What should be a sharp, affectionate send-up of 1950s creature features instead lands as a *toothless satire*—one that gestures toward genre parody without ever committing to genuine wit or bite. The references to classic monster movies feel more like decoration than commentary, and the film seems content to nod at its influences rather than say anything meaningful about them.

The plot compounds these problems. Loosely constructed and frequently incoherent, the story lurches from set piece to set piece with little regard for internal logic or, for that matter, the basic laws of physics. Action sequences unfold according to the demands of spectacle rather than sense, leaving audiences dazzled but disengaged. It's the kind of storytelling that assumes visual momentum can paper over narrative holes—an assumption that doesn't hold.

## Style Over Substance

No amount of celebrity voice talent or pop-culture winking can salvage this fundamental laziness. The star-studded cast, however capable, is asked to do the heavy lifting that the screenplay refuses to shoulder itself. And herein lies the defining weakness that continues to separate DreamWorks from its more disciplined competitors: where a studio like Pixar approaches storytelling with meticulous care—building coherent worlds, earning emotional beats, and respecting its audience's intelligence—DreamWorks too often settles for a lackadaisical approach that prioritizes noise and novelty over craft.

"Monsters vs. Aliens" is not without its charms, and younger viewers may well be entertained by its colorful chaos. But it remains a frustrating reminder of the gap between animation that merely fills the screen and animation that genuinely resonates.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN movie review of "Monsters vs. Aliens" (2009) from a critic who found it disappointing, in a witty and sarcastic voice, comparing it unfavorably to Pixar films.
counterfactuals.output:
# Monsters vs. Aliens: A Colossal Waste of Perfectly Good 3D Glasses

*By a critic who expected more than a 90-minute toy commercial*

DreamWorks Animation has once again proven that if you throw enough celebrity voices, explosions, and pop-culture references at a wall, some of it will stick—mostly to your popcorn-buttered fingers, and none of it to your memory.

"Monsters vs. Aliens" wants desperately to be an event. It arrives draped in cutting-edge 3D technology, as if depth perception alone could compensate for a script with all the emotional resonance of a cereal box. Spoiler alert: it cannot.

## A Premise in Search of a Point

Our heroine is Susan (Reese Witherspoon), a bride who gets zapped by a meteor on her wedding day and grows into a fifty-foot giant. It's a genuinely promising setup—a story about a woman literally too big for the small life others planned for her. For roughly eight minutes, I dared to hope.

Then the movie remembered it had a marketing department to please.

Susan is quickly filed away among a cabinet of "monster" sidekicks: a Jell-O blob named B.O.B. (Seth Rogen, playing a character whose entire personality is "has no brain," which the film mistakes for a running joke rather than an accurate review). There's a mad-scientist cockroach, a fish-ape hybrid, and a giant insect that exists mostly to be large. They are less characters than they are action figures awaiting their blister packaging.

## The Pixar Problem

Here's the uncomfortable comparison DreamWorks keeps inviting and losing: over at Pixar, they'd already given us a rat who dreams of Parisian cuisine and a mute robot who made us weep for a wilting plant. Those films understood a radical concept—that spectacle means nothing without a heartbeat.

"Monsters vs. Aliens" has the spectacle. What it lacks is anyone backstage who seems to care whether we feel anything. Where "WALL-E" trusted silence, this film panics at every quiet moment and immediately deploys another explosion or a Rogen ad-lib. It's the cinematic equivalent of a parent handing a screaming toddler an iPad.

## Style Without Substance

The animation, to be fair, is technically gorgeous. The 3D genuinely pops. San Francisco gets destroyed with real visual flair, and the alien overlord Gallaxhar (Rainn Wilson, gamely chewing digital scenery) is a nicely designed villain.

But gorgeous animation is now the *floor*, not the ceiling. Everyone can render a shiny explosion in 2009. What separates the great from the forgettable is whether you've written a single line anyone will quote next week. Try it. I'll wait.

## The Verdict

"Monsters vs. Aliens" isn't offensively bad. That would at least be interesting. It's something worse: aggressively fine. It's the film equivalent of a fast-food value meal—engineered, focus-grouped, momentarily satisfying, and utterly forgotten by the time you've thrown out the wrapper.

Your kids will enjoy it. They also enjoy eating glue. Set your standards accordingly.

**Rating: 2 out of 5 stars** — one for the animation, one because B.O.B. genuinely made me laugh once, which is one time more than the screenwriters apparently expected.

counterfactuals.output:
# "Monsters vs. Aliens" Squanders Its Promising Premise

There's a great movie hiding somewhere inside "Monsters vs. Aliens," DreamWorks Animation's 2009 3D spectacle. Unfortunately, you'll have to dig through a mountain of frantic action and half-baked jokes to find even a glimpse of it. What could have been a loving, clever tribute to 1950s creature features instead lands as a loud, forgettable exercise in style over substance.

## A Plot on Autopilot

The story follows Susan Murphy (voiced by Reese Witherspoon), a California bride who is struck by a meteorite on her wedding day and grows into a fifty-foot giantess. Captured by the government and renamed "Ginormica," she's imprisoned in a secret facility alongside a ragtag crew of other monsters. When an alien named Gallaxhar invades Earth in search of a powerful substance lodged in Susan's body, the monsters are unleashed to save the day.

It's a serviceable setup, but the screenplay treats it as little more than a clothesline on which to hang one action sequence after another. Susan's supposed arc—from timid pushover to empowered heroine—is telegraphed so bluntly and resolved so tidily that it carries zero emotional weight. The film keeps *telling* us she's finding her strength without ever earning the transformation. Every potentially interesting idea, from her broken engagement to the ethics of imprisoning sentient beings, gets steamrolled by the next chase or explosion.

## A Wasted Voice Cast

The vocal talent assembled here is genuinely impressive, which makes the results all the more frustrating. Witherspoon is perfectly pleasant as Susan, but she's given nothing memorable to do; her character is defined more by her size than by any personality. The supporting monsters fare a little better on paper: Hugh Laurie brings dignified warmth to the mad-scientist cockroach Dr. Cockroach, and Will Arnett is amusingly self-absorbed as the fish-ape hybrid The Missing Link. Seth Rogen's B.O.B.—a brainless blue blob—delivers a few genuine laughs, though his shtick wears thin by the halfway point.

The real casualties are Kiefer Sutherland's blustering General W.R. Monger and Stephen Colbert's dim-witted President, both of whom feel like they wandered in from a different, broader comedy. Rainn Wilson's villain Gallaxhar is all volume and no menace. With this caliber of cast, the flat writing feels less like a missed opportunity and more like an outright waste.

## References Without Reverence

"Monsters vs. Aliens" wants desperately to be seen as an homage to the golden age of B-movie sci-fi. The character designs nod to classics like "The Blob," "Attack of the 50 Foot Woman," "The Fly," and "Creature from the Black Lagoon." But nodding is all the film ever does. These references are surface-level costume choices, never woven into anything that comments on or celebrates the genre. A truly clever tribute would use these archetypes to say something; here, they're just recognizable shapes for kids to point at and adults to vaguely remember. The movie mistakes recognition for wit.

## Slick but Soulless Animation

If there's one area where the film delivers, it's the technical polish. Built as a showcase for the then-emerging 3D format, "Monsters vs. Aliens" is stuffed with objects hurled at the camera and vertiginous set pieces engineered purely to justify the glasses. The animation is undeniably smooth, the environments detailed, and Gallaxhar's spaceship interiors have a gleaming menace.

Yet the whole thing feels curiously weightless. The color palette is bright to the point of exhaustion, and the relentless motion never lets a single image breathe. Compared to the warmth and craftsmanship of Pixar's output in the same era, this looks like a very expensive theme-park ride—dazzling in the moment, hollow the instant it ends. Technical proficiency, it turns out, is no substitute for genuine artistry.

## The Verdict

"Monsters vs. Aliens" isn't offensively bad—it's something arguably worse: aggressively mediocre. It has the ingredients for something special (a fun premise, a stacked cast, a rich genre to mine) and does almost nothing interesting with any of them. Younger viewers may be entertained by the noise and color, but anyone hoping for the sharp wit or emotional resonance of the best animated films will leave hungry.

**Runtime:** 94 minutes
**Rating:** ★★☆☆☆ (2 out of 5)

# A Cautionary Tale from the Multiplex

**WARNING:** The following film contains dangerous levels of self-awareness, at least three plot holes large enough to swallow San Francisco whole, and a moral so gently delivered you'd need a seismograph to detect it. Viewer discretion—and possibly a strong cup of coffee—is advised.

DreamWorks' *Monsters vs. Aliens* arrives with the confidence of a movie that has seen *The Blob*, *The Fly*, and *Godzilla*, took careful notes, then decided to blend them into a smoothie and serve it to seven-year-olds. To be fair, it's a *tasty* smoothie. But let's not pretend we're dining on caviar.

Our heroine, Susan, gets zapped by a meteor on her wedding day and balloons into a fifty-foot woman—a plot the 1958 B-movie schlock-classic *Attack of the 50 Ft. Woman* already handled with more camp and considerably less merchandising potential. Susan spends the film "finding herself," which apparently requires becoming a giant, punching an alien robot, and dumping her spineless weatherman fiancé. It's *empowerment*, you see: the kind where a woman only discovers her worth after literally outgrowing every man in her life. Subtle as a monster stomping through downtown.

The film's logic operates on what I can only call *convenience physics*. Susan's size fluctuates whenever the script requires a sight gag. The government has apparently been housing monsters for fifty years but only NOW decides to deploy them. And the alien overlord Gallaxhar—voiced with delicious ham by Rainn Wilson—clones himself into an army, yet somehow can't manage to defeat one confused newlywed. One suspects the screenwriters, like Gallaxhar's clones, were simply too numerous to coordinate.

And yet—damn them—it *works*. B.O.B., the brainless blue gelatinous blob, is a stroke of comedic genius, a loving wink at every drive-in creature feature that ever oozed across a screen. Dr. Cockroach tips his hat to Vincent Price. The whole affair is a valentine to the monster movies your grandparents feared and your parents mocked.

**Verdict:** *Monsters vs. Aliens* is loud, dumb, occasionally clever, and never quite as smart as it thinks it is. Rather like the alien invasion it depicts, it's flashy, formulaic, and ultimately defeated by its own overreach. Bring the kids. Lower your expectations. Enjoy the blob.

★★★ out of five giant, radioactive stars.

counterfactuals.output:
# When Size Matters: "Monsters vs. Aliens" Delivers Fun in a Bigger Dimension

DreamWorks Animation has never been shy about its ambitions, and with "Monsters vs. Aliens," the studio swings for the fences with a candy-colored, retro-inspired romp that mostly connects. Directed by Rob Letterman and Conrad Vernon, this affectionate homage to 1950s creature features arrives wrapped in cutting-edge 3-D technology and buoyed by a voice cast stacked with comedic talent. The result is a film that, while narratively slight, charms through sheer exuberance and technical wizardry.

## A Heroine Worth Rooting For

At the center is Susan Murphy, voiced with disarming warmth by Reese Witherspoon. On her wedding day, poor Susan is struck by a meteorite and inconveniently grows to nearly fifty feet tall. Whisked away by the government and rebranded "Ginormica," she's imprisoned alongside a menagerie of misfit monsters. Witherspoon grounds the fantastical proceedings with genuine emotional stakes, transforming what could have been a one-note gag into a surprisingly resonant coming-into-her-own story. Susan's arc—from apologetic doormat to confident heroine—gives the film a feminist backbone that distinguishes it from lazier animated fare.

The screenplay understands that Susan's growth is metaphorical as much as physical. Her wishy-washy fiancé, a self-absorbed weatherman named Derek, represents everything she must outgrow, and Witherspoon sells both the heartbreak and the eventual liberation with admirable nuance.

## The Monster Mash

The supporting monsters provide the film's most reliable laughs. Seth Rogen is perfectly cast as B.O.B., a brainless blue blob of indeterminate gelatinous origin. Rogen's stoner-adjacent delivery makes B.O.B.'s cheerful idiocy endlessly quotable, and his obliviousness serves as the movie's comedic engine. Whether professing love to a bowl of Jell-O or misunderstanding basic concepts, B.O.B. steals nearly every scene he oozes into.

Rounding out the crew are Hugh Laurie as the mad-scientist cockroach Dr. Cockroach, Ph.D., and Will Arnett as the fish-ape hybrid The Missing Link. Laurie brings theatrical relish to his role, while Arnett's washed-up bravado provides steady chuckles. The gigantic, silent Insectosaurus completes this endearing ensemble.

## Colbert's Commander-in-Chief

Stephen Colbert nearly walks away with the entire picture as President Hathaway, a buffoonish commander-in-chief whose response to alien contact involves attempting to communicate through a keyboard rendition of "Axel F." Colbert's gift for portraying pompous authority figures serves him beautifully here, and his handful of scenes crackle with satirical energy. It's a reminder that well-cast comedic actors can elevate even modest material.

The alien threat comes courtesy of Gallaxhar, voiced by Rainn Wilson with gleeful megalomania. While the villain remains fairly standard-issue, Wilson injects enough manic enthusiasm to keep him entertaining. Kiefer Sutherland also appears as the gruff General W.R. Monger, chewing scenery with gravelly gusto.

## The Third Dimension

Where "Monsters vs. Aliens" truly justifies its existence is in its 3-D presentation. DreamWorks reportedly designed the film from the ground up for the format, and the difference shows. Rather than the murky, headache-inducing gimmickry of lesser 3-D efforts, this film uses depth thoughtfully. A paddle-ball sequence early in the film gleefully thrusts objects toward the audience, while the vast alien landscapes achieve genuine grandeur through layered perspective.

The 3-D adds tangible dimension to action set pieces, particularly a thrilling chase across the Golden Gate Bridge that ranks among the film's highlights. Viewers with access to a properly equipped theater should absolutely seek out the enhanced version; the standard 2-D presentation, while perfectly watchable, sacrifices a significant portion of the spectacle that makes the film special.

## The Verdict

"Monsters vs. Aliens" is not without flaws. The plot follows a predictable trajectory, and the second act sags under the weight of familiar animated-movie conventions. Some jokes aim squarely at parents' nostalgia, occasionally leaving younger viewers behind, while others skew too juvenile for adults.

Yet these quibbles hardly sink an enterprise this good-natured. Anchored by Witherspoon's heartfelt performance, propelled by Rogen's comic timing, and elevated by Colbert's political lampooning, the film delivers exactly what it promises: colorful, energetic family entertainment with a genuinely progressive message tucked inside its retro packaging.

In an era of increasingly cynical children's films, there's something refreshing about a movie this eager to please. Bigger, it turns out, can indeed be better.

**★★★ (out of four)**

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an entertainment column review panning "Monsters vs. Aliens," noting its high-concept premise, weak plot, strong female lead Ginormica, and how it stacks up against "Coraline" and "Space Chimps."
counterfactuals.output:
# When Bigger Isn't Better: "Monsters vs. Aliens" Falls Flat

There's a moment early in "Monsters vs. Aliens" when you sense exactly what this movie wants to be: a clever, high-concept romp that takes the dusty tropes of 1950s creature features and blasts them into the 3-D age. The pitch practically writes itself—a ragtag band of government-detained monsters gets deployed to save Earth from an alien invasion. It's the kind of premise that sells itself in a single sentence. If only the movie itself were half as sharp as its logline.

## A Premise in Search of a Plot

DreamWorks Animation has always been the class clown to Pixar's valedictorian, and here the studio leans hard into spectacle at the expense of storytelling. The trouble isn't the concept—it's that nobody bothered to build much underneath it. The narrative lurches from set piece to set piece with all the structural integrity of a Jell-O mold, coasting on frantic action and pop-culture winks rather than anything resembling genuine stakes. Characters are introduced, given a single defining gag, and then wheeled out whenever the pacing sags.

By the third act, you feel the machinery grinding: explosion, quip, explosion, sentimental beat, explosion. It's exhausting rather than exhilarating.

## The One Bright Spot

If there's a reason to buy a ticket, her name is Ginormica. Susan Murphy—transformed on her wedding day into a fifty-foot force of nature—is a genuinely refreshing heroine, and the film's emotional core lives almost entirely in her journey from doormat bride-to-be to self-possessed powerhouse. Her arc, from apologizing for her own existence to embracing her extraordinary size, gives the movie a beating heart it doesn't otherwise earn. That she towers over her supporting cast is fitting; she's the only character with any real dimension.

The problem is that the surrounding menagerie—a gelatinous blob, a mad-scientist cockroach, a Missing Link—too often reduce her to straight-man duty amid their scattershot antics.

## The Competition

Here's where "Monsters vs. Aliens" really suffers: it arrived in a season that showed what animation could do. Set it beside Henry Selick's "Coraline," and the comparison is almost cruel. "Coraline" understood that 3-D could be atmosphere rather than gimmick, that children's stories could carry genuine unease and craftsmanship. Every frame felt handmade and intentional. "Monsters vs. Aliens," by contrast, treats its depth-of-field as a rollercoaster—come look at the paddleball flying at your face!—and little more.

To be fair, this is no "Space Chimps," that bargain-bin misfire that gave animated space adventures a bad name. "Monsters vs. Aliens" is glossier, funnier, and infinitely better produced. But "we're better than 'Space Chimps'" is not exactly a ringing endorsement to print on the poster.

## The Verdict

There's a good movie buried somewhere in "Monsters vs. Aliens"—you can glimpse it whenever Ginormica commands the screen. But high concept can only carry you so far, and this one runs out of gas long before the credits roll. It's loud, it's colorful, and it will keep the kids occupied. It just won't stay with them, or you, past the parking lot.

**★★ out of five.** A monster of a premise, undone by an alien lack of story.
